package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to 3.2.2 and 4.1 are affected (e.g., 3.2.1, 4.0).
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2015-6420) that enables remote code execution (RCE) when untrusted data is deserialized. Attackers can exploit gadget chains in vulnerable versions to execute arbitrary code on the host system, posing a severe risk to any application that deserializes untrusted input using this library.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when the application deserializes untrusted data using ObjectInputStream or similar APIs.
execution_context.file_location: Any Java application code path that invokes ObjectInputStream.readObject() or similar deserialization methods, especially in web controllers, API endpoints, or file upload handlers.
required_permissions: Read access to input stream (e.g., file, network socket, HTTP request body)
Network access (if deserialization is triggered by remote input)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(inputStream);
Object obj = ois.readObject();
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: This code deserializes an object from an input stream. If the input contains a maliciously crafted serialized payload that leverages gadget chains in vulnerable versions of commons-collections, arbitrary code execution can be triggered during deserialization.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted data using ObjectInputStream in the presence of vulnerable commons-collections versions is highly dangerous. Attackers can craft serialized objects that exploit known gadget chains, resulting in arbitrary code execution without any user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal deserialization expects only safe, trusted objects to be reconstructed. Here, deserialization of attacker-controlled data can trigger execution of code embedded in the payload, violating the expectation of data integrity and code safety.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deserialization is legitimate when used with trusted, validated data sources and when class whitelisting or object validation is enforced. For example, restoring application state from a secure, internal file.
key_indicators: Deserialization of data from untrusted or external sources
Use of ObjectInputStream.readObject() without input validation or class whitelisting
Presence of vulnerable commons-collections versions (prior to 3.2.2 or 4.1) in the classpath
Loading or instantiation of known gadget classes (e.g., org.apache.commons.collections.functors.InvokerTransformer) during deserialization

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious serialized Java payload that exploits commons-collections gadget chains and delivers it to the application (e.g., via HTTP POST, file upload, or other input vectors).
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives the malicious payload and prepares to process it.

attack_chain.action: Application deserializes the untrusted payload using ObjectInputStream and vulnerable commons-collections classes, triggering the gadget chain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of attacker-controlled code on the server during deserialization.

attack_chain.action: Attacker achieves remote code execution on the target system, potentially installing malware, exfiltrating data, or moving laterally within the network.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full compromise of the application and possible escalation within the environment.

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of data from untrusted or external sources using ObjectInputStream or similar APIs
Loading or instantiation of commons-collections gadget classes (e.g., InvokerTransformer, ChainedTransformer) during deserialization
Unexpected process creation, command execution, or network activity immediately following deserialization events
file_indicators: Presence of commons-collections-3.2.1.jar, commons-collections-4.0.jar, or other vulnerable versions in application dependencies
Application code invoking ObjectInputStream.readObject() or similar methods on data from external sources (e.g., HTTP request, uploaded file) without validation
Absence of class whitelisting or object validation in deserialization code paths
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests or file uploads containing serialized Java objects (binary data with Java serialization headers, e.g., AC ED 00 05)
Outbound network connections or callbacks initiated by the application process immediately after deserialization
Unusual traffic patterns or connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure following deserialization events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static analysis to identify code paths that deserialize data from external or untrusted sources using ObjectInputStream or similar APIs. Flag applications bundling vulnerable versions of commons-collections (prior to 3.2.2 or 4.1) for immediate review. Monitor runtime logs for loading of known gadget classes and for unexpected process or network activity following deserialization. Use network monitoring to detect inbound serialized Java objects and outbound connections triggered by deserialization. Enforce input validation, class whitelisting, and upgrade to patched library versions to mitigate risk.
